world.bio: I delivered babies in Manchester for thirty-one years, the last nine of them as a practice educator training student midwives. I retired in June. My husband says I now spend my days reorganising the spare room, and he is not wrong. I have two grown children and a granddaughter due in March. I do not know what to do with my afternoons.
skills_assets: Thirty-one years of clinical midwifery, including community and labour ward work
Nine years as a practice educator: supervising students, writing competency assessments, debriefing difficult births
A box of teaching materials I wrote myself: case discussions, a laminated card for shoulder dystocia, a checklist for postnatal home visits
A friendly relationship with a few midwifery lecturers I used to meet at placement reviews
An allotment plot in Chorlton, overrun with courgettes
Very little tolerance for jargon and none for rushing a first-time mother

projects.name: Honorary teaching post at the university
projects.text: Over the summer I offered to tutor student midwives at the university for free: two afternoons a week, small groups, practical skills and reflective sessions. I wrote the email myself and copied in a lecturer I know. They replied warmly that there was no budget for an honorary post, and that the paperwork for volunteers to work with students had stalled in HR. That was in July. It is now October, and the lecturer has stopped answering my follow-ups. I feel foolish for even asking.

projects.name: The spare room
projects.text: Reorganising the spare room into a study for my granddaughter's visits. I have sorted three decades of paperwork into four boxes and thrown away a surprising amount. I keep finding old student reflective journals that I was meant to return and never did. I am reading them again and getting a bit misty.

notes.text: Found a student's reflective journal from 2019 in a box in the spare room. She wrote about her first stillbirth: how she did not know where to put her hands and how I held her elbow without saying anything. I had forgotten. I sat on the floor and read all twenty pages. Thirty-one years of babies and I had forgotten the one that mattered to her.

Allotment day. The courgettes have gone feral. I gave away eleven to neighbours and left four on the bench for strangers. A young woman took one and said, 'I've never cooked these.' I said I'd show her a recipe. Standing there with a marrow in my hands I thought: this is what retirement is, giving people vegetables.

Rob's band played at The Crown. Three songs were new. I know all the words to the old ones and none to the new ones. He bought me a gin and said, 'Mum, you don't have to come to every one.' I said I know. I went anyway. I will go to every one.

Spanish app, Duolingo owl is sending me passive-aggressive notifications. I am going to Valencia in November with my sister and I want to order dinner without pointing. I can say 'una mesa para dos' and 'la cuenta, por favor'. That's it. We will starve politely.

Phoned the lecturer again. Voicemail. I realise I am treating a rejected offer like a patient I haven't seen for a while. I keep wanting to check in. But you cannot make people accept your help; I tell students that. It does not feel the same when it is you.

Went to the memorial for a colleague who died in August. Forty midwives in one room, half of whom I trained or worked with. Several asked what I was doing now. I said 'allotment and Spanish'. They laughed. One of them, a young one, quietly said she wished I could still be on the ward to talk her through bad days. I kept that sentence all week.

My daughter-in-law is thirty weeks. She asked if I could come to the antenatal class with her. I said of course, and then spent the evening wondering whether I would be able to stay quiet. Retired midwives make terrible birth partners because we know too much.

Wrote a 'what I would teach' list on the back of an envelope: how to ask permission before touching; how to say 'I don't know yet'; how to write notes that another midwife can read at 3 am; how to leave a room when you are about to cry. Sixteen items. Put it in the drawer with the other envelope lists.

Chorlton farmers' market. Bought sourdough and a jar of damson jam. The woman who sold it to me is a former patient. She had her first baby with me in 1998. She said, 'Mrs Hale, he's a barrister now.' I said, 'Don't tell me, I'll cry on your stall.' I cried on her stall.

messages.text:
Alan: You've been in that spare room for four hours.
Me: I'm sorting.
Alan: You're reading.
Me: Those are the same thing, Alan.
Alan: I'm making tea. Do you want any?
Me: Yes please. And a biscuit.

Brenda: Valencia: do we have the flights sorted?
Me: Booked. Fourteenth of November.
Brenda: And how's the Spanish?
Me: Una mesa para dos.
Brenda: God help us.

Aisha: Would you really come to the antenatal class?
Me: Of course. I'll sit at the back and keep my mouth shut.
Aisha: You won't.
Me: No, I won't.
Aisha: Good. I'd rather you didn't.

Dr. Patel: Maureen, sorry for the slow reply. HR still hasn't cleared volunteers. I'm not sure it will happen this year.
Me: That's all right. I understand.
Dr. Patel: I do wish we could have you in.
Me: So do I. Take care.

relations.about: Retired bus inspector, calm, makes tea whenever I go quiet.
Plays guitar in a pub band, works in logistics, kind to a fault.
Thirty weeks pregnant, first baby, a bit anxious.
University lecturer and a friend; wants me in but can't make HR move.

constraints: Cannot commit to weekdays before 4 pm outside school terms
Will not work without clear boundaries about supervision
Not interested in being paid for it
Dislike travel for more than a day
sensitive: I miss the ward more than I tell anyone
I have been low since August and put it down to the weather
